title: Why bodies? Twelve reasons for including bodily expressions in affective neuroscience
key_findings: Over 95% of human emotion studies had used faces; a May-2009 PubMed count gave 3521 hits for emotion x faces vs 339 for emotion x bodies.
Bodily expressions are recognised about as reliably as facial expressions; dynamic clips are recognised roughly 10% better than stills; point-light displays are harder.
Bodies show emotion together with the action the person is preparing (fear body = escape) and can be read at a distance where faces cannot.
Body emotion biases how an ambiguous face is read; face-body incongruence is detected early (~115 ms).
Different emotions draw attention to different body parts (e.g. hands for aggression).
practical_applications: Faceless characters (Mint & Tao) can carry emotion through posture and movement; this is a research-backed channel, not a workaround.
Show the action tendency (approach, withdraw, freeze) rather than a static 'emotion pose'.
limitations: Narrative review by one author, partly built on her own lab's work; neuroscience parts are not directly needed for craft.
WebFetch read ~100k of ~116k characters (the end of the reference list not read).
license: open access via PMC (Royal Society; check licence)

title: Emotion expression in body action and posture
authors: Dael, N.; Mortillaro, M.; Scherer, K. R.
key_findings: 10 professional actors x 12 emotions (GEMEP corpus), coded with the Body Action and Posture (BAP) system and reduced to 16 behaviour factors.
Hot anger was homogeneously expressed by frontal body lean / forward movement (one cluster contained all hot-anger portrayals).
Amusement: touching/manipulation and discontinuous movements with mid-action holds, head straight and oriented to the interlocutor.
Elated joy (70%) and pride (40%) shared symmetrical up-down repetitive arm action; panic fear (60%) shared symmetrical arm action with knee movement, overlapping with joy (30%).

Sadness (60%) and relief (50%) were grouped together by arms resting (in pockets); despair and anxiety shared an indistinct pattern; anxiety + panic fear also showed backward lean, upward gaze and lateral trunk lean.
Interest and irritation shared arms at side + trunk leaning forward + one-arm asymmetric action.
Discriminant classification: elated joy 90%, amusement and hot anger 70%, sadness and irritation 30%; sadness was classified as despair as often as sadness. Cross-validated accuracies only 10-60%.
Arousal (activation) was the first discriminating dimension; most emotions were expressed by several different patterns.
practical_applications: High-arousal emotions (anger, joy, amusement) are easy to stage with body alone; low-arousal ones (sadness vs relief, irritation vs interest) need context, props or a second cue.
Disambiguate pairs known to be confused: joy vs panic fear, sadness vs relief vs despair, interest vs irritation.
limitations: Acted portrayals by 10 Western-European actors, standing, filmed in a lab; not spontaneous behaviour.
Exploratory cluster analysis; small n per cell; classification not cross-validated in the main report.

title: Affective Body Expression Perception and Recognition: A Survey
key_findings: Both form (posture) and motion carry affect; motion can be sufficient for basic emotions but recognition drops when form is disrupted; posture helps separate emotions with similar movement activation.
High-level features that matter: leaning direction, openness of the body, head position (up/down/tilted); angular/diagonal configurations read as threatening, rounded ones as warm (Aronoff, ballet).
Sadness core: arms straight down close to the body; happiness/elation: head bent back, arms often raised; hands raised = happy, low = sad; lateral opening separates happy and fear from sad.
Disgust and pride can both use crossed arms; head position separates them (forward for disgust, back for pride) - Wallbott.

Non-acted Wii postures: defeated and concentrating both had slumped shoulders and arms down/diagonal; frustrated and triumphant both had shoulders up/back and arms raised laterally - arousal separated better than valence.
Cross-cultural: Japanese, Sri Lankan and American observers agreed best on sad/depressed for a faceless genderless avatar, but Japanese rated animated postures as more intense.
Prototypical expressions are rare in real life (Russell); context changes how an emotion is expressed.
practical_applications: Use head position + openness + lean as the three main levers for a faceless puppet.
Expect triumph vs frustration and defeat vs concentration to be confused unless context or hands disambiguate.
limitations: Narrative survey (not systematic); most cited studies use acted expressions.
Read from a lecture-site copy of the published PDF; tables partly garbled in text extraction.

title: Emotion perception from dynamic and static body expressions in point-light and full-light displays
authors: Atkinson, A. P.; Dittrich, W. H.; Gemmell, A. J.; Young, A. W.
key_findings: 10 actors with faces covered portrayed anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness at 3 levels of exaggeration; 150 full-light and 150 point-light clips plus static peak frames.
Basic emotions were readily identified from body movement even in point-light displays; static images were less efficient than dynamic displays.

More exaggerated movement increased recognition accuracy (most clearly for dynamic point-light) and intensity ratings; intensity judgements relied more on movement than on static form (secondary summaries add: exaggeration did not help sadness).
practical_applications: Faces can be hidden entirely and emotion still reads - direct support for faceless characters.
In clips, exaggerate movement amplitude for clarity; in stills (carousels) expect lower accuracy and add context.
limitations: Abstract read via Europe PMC; per-emotion accuracies not read.
Acted, Western actors.

title: Perception of emotion from dynamic point-light displays represented in dance
authors: Dittrich, W. H.; Troscianko, T.; Lea, S. E. G.; Morgan, D.
key_findings: Two trained dancers conveyed fear, anger, grief, joy, surprise, disgust.
Full-body clips: 88% correct; upright point-light (13 dots): 63% correct, well above chance; inversion reduced point-light performance close to chance.
practical_applications: Movement pattern alone carries emotion - a simplified stick/pencil figure that moves well can read.
Keep characters upright and anatomically coherent; scrambled or inverted motion loses meaning.
limitations: Only two dancers; dance is stylised movement.
Abstract only.

title: Body cues, not facial expressions, discriminate between intense positive and negative emotions
authors: Aviezer, H.; Trope, Y.; Todorov, A.
key_findings: At peak intensity (e.g. winning/losing), positive and negative situations were discriminated from isolated bodies but not from isolated faces.
Viewers perceived illusory valence in non-diagnostic faces when shown with bodies; in face-body composites, perceived affect followed the body.
practical_applications: For big moments (win, loss, shock) the body pose decides how the moment reads - design the body first.
Body + context can make the same neutral/ambiguous face (or no face) read as joy or despair.
limitations: Real-life photos of athletes/people at peak intensity; generalisation to mild emotions not tested.
Abstract only.

title: Attributing emotion to static body postures: Recognition accuracy, confusions, and viewpoint dependence
key_findings: 176 computer-generated mannequin postures, each from 3 viewing angles, forced choice of 6 emotions.
Agreement ranged from zero for many disgust postures to over 90% for some anger and sadness postures.
Anatomical features and viewing angle predicted responses; confusions suggested a circumplex, with happiness and surprise close together.
practical_applications: For static images of simplified figures: anger and sadness can read from posture alone; disgust needs props/context.
Pick the camera angle that shows the posture most clearly (viewpoint matters).
limitations: Wooden, faceless mannequins without hand detail; static only.
Abstract read; per-feature tables not read.

title: Perceiving affect from arm movement
authors: Pollick, F. E.; Paterson, H. M.; Bruderlin, A.; Sanford, A. J.
key_findings: Point-light drinking and knocking arm movements with 10 affects; perceived affect formed a circumplex: dimension 1 activation, dimension 2 pleasantness.
Activation correlated strongly with movement kinematics (speed) even in scrambled displays; pleasantness seemed carried by phase relations between limb segments.
Secondary summaries: anger/happiness judged from fast, jerky movement; sadness from slow, smooth movement.
practical_applications: Tempo controls arousal: speed up for anger/joy/excitement, slow and smooth for sadness/tiredness.
Valence needs coordination quality (smooth flowing vs jerky, disconnected), not just speed.
limitations: Two actors; arm-only point-light.
Abstract only; the fast/jerky detail comes from secondary sources.

title: Critical features for the perception of emotion from gait
authors: Roether, C. L.; Omlor, L.; Christensen, A.; Giese, M. A.
key_findings: Motion capture of neutral, angry, happy, sad, fearful gaits from 25 people; observers judged avatars animated with them.
Judgements rely on simple features such as overall speed and on posture/dynamic cues; emotion-specific features depended on only a few joints.
Artificial walkers with only the critical features produced after-effects like natural emotional walkers.
practical_applications: A walk cycle can carry emotion with a few changes: speed, head inclination, arm-swing amplitude (details in the Kleinsmith survey).
Matches rig.js walk timings (brisk vs slow) - a cheap emotion channel for every entrance.
limitations: Abstract only; exact joint-angle results not read.
Acted gaits.
license: open access (Journal of Vision; check licence)

title: Bodily expression of emotion
key_findings: (Per Dael2012 and Kleinsmith2013, which were read in full) Actors portraying 14 emotions; overall classification ~.54; movement quality (activity, expansiveness, energy) strongly aided differentiation.

(Per secondary sources) part of the movement differences are explained by activation; collapsed posture for shame/sadness; pride more in body than face; arms crossed for disgust and pride, separated by head forward vs back.
practical_applications: Use expansiveness and energy as first-order controls; head position as the tie-breaker.
limitations: Not read directly; findings stated only as reported by secondary sources.

title: The spontaneous expression of pride and shame: Evidence for biologically innate nonverbal displays
key_findings: Judo athletes at the 2004 Olympic (sighted, 36 nations) and Paralympic (blind, 20 nations, 12 congenitally blind) Games.
After winning: head tilted back, smile, arms raised, hands in fists, arms out, chest expanded, torso out - in sighted and blind athletes; hands on hips NOT reliably displayed.
After losing: only shoulders slumped and chest narrowed increased (head down / face hiding not associated with losing in this photo set).
Shame display was weaker in more individualistic cultures (sighted only), suggesting cultural suppression; no moderation in blind athletes.
practical_applications: Triumph = expand and rise (head back, arms up/out, fists); defeat = narrow the chest, drop the shoulders.
In collectivist settings (including Thai audiences, plausibly) visible shame displays after failure are culturally acceptable - but this is an inference, Thailand not separately analysed.
limitations: No self-report of felt emotion; competition with audience; one photographer, limited angles; small congenitally blind sample.

title: How do we recognize emotion from movement? Specific motor components contribute to the recognition of each emotion
authors: Melzer, A.; Shafir, T.; Tsachor, R. P.
key_findings: Earlier work (Shafir et al. 2016) found Laban components that enhanced feeling: happiness = jumping, rhythmic, spreading, free flow, lightness, up, rising; sadness = passive weight, arms touching upper body, sinking, head dropping; fear = retreating, condensing, bound flow, backwards, enclosing; anger = strong weight, sudden time, advancing, direct.
Clips of Certified Movement Analysts moving those components (without intending emotion) were recognised as the associated emotion above chance; anger only 47.2% of anger-component clips.
Actor clips (Atkinson set) were recognised better for anger, fear and neutral.
practical_applications: A practical vocabulary for directing movement quality: e.g. 'sinking, passive weight' for sadness; 'retreat + condense + bound flow' for fear.
Useful prompt words for AI video and notes for puppet timing.
limitations: All movers adult Caucasian women; sample too small for cross-cultural analysis; Laban coding by its own practitioners.

title: Assessing the reliability of the Laban Movement Analysis system
authors: Bernardet, U.; Fdili Alaoui, S.; Studd, K.; Bradley, K.; Pasquier, P.; Schiphorst, T.
key_findings: Certified Movement Analysts annotated the most and second-most salient difference between a neutral and a varied movement in a custom tool.
Inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha) ranged from weak to acceptable depending on how the two rounds were combined.
Positioned as the first formal reliability assessment of a widely used system.
practical_applications: Treat Laban terms as a shared craft vocabulary, not as a validated measurement scale.
When two people disagree about Laban labels for a shot, that is normal - test with viewers instead.
limitations: One study, small expert sample, limited movement set.

title: Do the eyes have it? Cues to the direction of social attention
authors: Langton, S. R. H.; Watt, R. J.; Bruce, V.
key_findings: Gaze direction is processed rapidly and triggers reflexive shifts of the observer's attention, even when uninformative and when told to ignore it.
Perceived attention direction depends not only on the eyes but on head orientation, body posture and pointing; head orientation changes perceived gaze (Wollaston effect).
Head orientation and pointing may be more salient than eye gaze for young children; cues are processed automatically and in parallel.
practical_applications: Faceless characters can still 'look': turn the head (and body) toward the target and the viewer's attention follows.
Use head turn + point to steer the viewer to a product or object in the frame.
limitations: Review written 2000; later gaze-cueing literature not covered here.
license: author accepted manuscript (University of Stirling repository)

title: The eyes have it: the neuroethology, function and evolution of social gaze
key_findings: Gaze is a core social signal; its signal value depends on the status, disposition and emotional state of sender and receiver.
Brain regions respond selectively to faces, bodies and gaze; gaze following may be 'hard-wired' (STS-amygdala-OFC circuit).
practical_applications: Direct orientation toward another character = engagement/challenge; averted = deference/avoidance - read through status context.
limitations: Abstract only; mostly primate neuroethology.

title: The many faces of a neutral face: Head tilt and perception of dominance and emotion
key_findings: Secondary sources disagree on what it found: one says direct gaze + upward head tilt expresses dominance and downward head + averted gaze submission; another attributes 'head down increases perceived dominance' to it.

Later work (2020, Perception, per search snippet) found both 30-degree up and 20-degree down postures read as more dominant and less trustworthy than level; Witkower & Tracy reported slightly-down heads read angrier.
practical_applications: Head pitch changes perceived status and emotion, but the direction depends on the rest of the face/body and the camera angle - test, do not assume.
limitations: Not read; secondary sources conflict - recorded as contested.

title: Bodily communication of emotion: Evidence for extrafacial behavioral expressions and available coding systems
key_findings: (Abstract per search result) Reviews evidence that pride, joy, sadness, shame, embarrassment, anger, fear and disgust are shown and recognised through bodily behaviour.
No existing body coding system covers the full range of emotions.
practical_applications: Supports a pose library covering these eight emotions as the most evidence-backed set.
limitations: Abstract content seen only via search result text.

title: When do gestures communicate? A meta-analysis
key_findings: 63 samples: speech + gesture gives a significant, moderate comprehension benefit over speech alone.
Gestures depicting motor actions help more than gestures about abstract topics.
Benefit is larger when gestures are not redundant with speech; children benefit more than adults.
practical_applications: Give characters gestures that add information (show the size, shape, action) rather than repeat the words.
In TTS clips, an iconic gesture of the action described helps viewers - especially for family/child audiences.
limitations: Abstract only; lab comprehension tasks.

title: The prosodic characteristics of non-referential co-speech gestures in a sample of academic-lecture-style speech
key_findings: Summarises McNeill (1992): referential gestures = iconic, metaphoric, deictic; beats were defined mainly as 'not iconic, metaphoric or deictic'; McNeill distinguished single flick beats marking narrative points from rhythm-beating gestures.

1,334 stroke-defined gestures in 20 min of lecture speech: the stroke of non-referential gestures tends to align with a pitch-accented syllable, as for other gesture types (Loehr 2004 strokes align with pitch accents).
Cites Kendon (1972, 1980, 2004) for gesture phrase structure and kinematic constancy across prosodic constituents; non-referential gestures are not a homogeneous 'beat' class.
practical_applications: Time a gesture's stroke to the stressed syllable of the TTS line; preparation before, hold/retraction after.
Use beats sparingly as emphasis; use iconic gestures for content.
limitations: One speaker style (American English lectures); Thai is a tonal language - stroke-to-stress alignment in Thai not tested here.

title: Hand and Mind: What Gestures Reveal about Thought
key_findings: (Per secondary sources read: ShattuckHufnagelRen2018 and search results) Classifies co-speech gestures as iconic, metaphoric, deictic and beats; categories are not mutually exclusive; builds on 'Kendon's continuum'.
practical_applications: Plan each gesture by type: show (iconic), idea-as-object (metaphoric), point (deictic), emphasis (beat).
limitations: Book not read; content stated only as reported by secondary sources.

title: Preferred interpersonal distances: A global comparison
authors: Sorokowska, A.; Sorokowski, P.; Hilpert, P.; et al.
key_findings: 8,943 participants in 42 countries chose preferred distances on a 0-220 cm graphic scale between two figures (stranger, acquaintance, close person).
Means: social (stranger) 135.1 cm, personal (acquaintance) 91.7 cm, intimate (close) 31.9 cm; the order held in every country, absolute values varied widely.
Women and older people preferred larger distances; warmer countries preferred closer stranger distances.
Hall's (1966) contact/non-contact split by geography (Asian populations as non-contact) is only partly supported; earlier evidence was often anecdotal.
Thailand was not among the sampled countries (checked the manuscript text).
practical_applications: Distance between Mint and Tao in frame is a relationship dial: ~1 body-width apart = close; 2-3 = acquainted; more = stranger/estranged.
Do not rely on Hall's culture labels; use the relative order, which is cross-culturally stable.
limitations: Self-report picture task, not observed behaviour; sex of the other person unspecified; ~200 per country.
license: accepted manuscript, WRAP terms (personal research use)

title: The Hidden Dimension
key_findings: (Per Sorokowska2017, read in full) Proposes four distance zones - intimate (0-46 cm), personal, social and public - and a contact vs non-contact culture distinction; cultural norms seen as the main factor.
practical_applications: Zone vocabulary for staging two-shots and for blocking real people in clips.
limitations: Not read; zone ranges beyond 'intimate 0-46 cm' not confirmed this session; theory partly anecdotal (Sorokowska2017).

title: Thai Traditional Salutation
key_findings: Wai: palms joined, touching the body between face and chest; the higher the hands, the greater the respect; the junior in age or rank initiates and the senior reciprocates; less strict between intimates.
Movement is never sharp: raised and lowered gracefully, upper arms close to the body, elbows not extended; idealised hand shape is the 'budding lotus' (phanom mue).
A senior conscious of superiority returns the wai no higher than the chest, or just nods / raises the right hand (rap wai); monks do not return a layperson's wai.
When standing before a seated respected person one stoops or bends the head; simple folk crouch on their haunches before great personages until they pass.

Krap (kneel and bow, forehead to floor between the hands, three times) is for the Buddha/Triple Gems; mop krap (crouched bow) for parents, teachers, royalty; side-sitting posture 'nang phap phiap' with legs folded back.
The author stresses variation by class, locality and setting; his description is a generalisation.
practical_applications: Correct Thai respect choreography for characters: who wais first, hand height by status, slow tempo, elbows in.
A rushed, high-elbow or one-handed wai reads as careless or comic - use only on purpose.
limitations: Mid-20th-century description (exact year not confirmed); modern urban practice is looser (Thailand Foundation and guides).
Scanned text with OCR errors.

title: Feet Low, Head High: A Guide to Thai Etiquettes
key_findings: Feet are the lowest/least clean part: do not point feet or soles at people or Buddha images; tuck feet or sit cross-legged; do not put feet on tables; do not step over pillows or books.
Head is the most sacred part: do not touch anyone's head, even children's; do not pass objects over a head; bow the head when walking past elders.
Do not position the body above an elder's head; crouch or move on knees to pass seated elders or monks.
Everyday wai: palms together at chest level with a slight head bow; on special occasions bow low with hands at the elder's feet.
practical_applications: Cultural checks for every Thai scene: feet direction when seated, no head pats, lower the body when passing elders.
limitations: Cultural-promotion article (states it does not reflect government views); normative, not observational.

title: Facial Action Coding System (FACS) - product page
key_findings: FACS is an anatomically based system describing all visually discernible facial movement as Action Units; first published 1978 (Ekman & Friesen), revised 2002.
FACS codes are descriptive; EMFACS codes 'have to be interpreted into emotion categories'.
Self-study 50-100 hours; used by researchers, animators and computer scientists.
practical_applications: Use AU names as a precise vocabulary for faces when a character HAS a face (TTS clip puppets, AI video prompts), not as an emotion detector.
limitations: Vendor page.

title: Model for predicting perception of facial action unit activation using virtual humans
authors: McDonnell, R.; Zibrek, K.; Carrigan, E.; Dahyot, R.
key_findings: Blendshape rigs are usually built from FACS Action Units; some AUs are perceptually more noticeable than others (ordering table provided).
Perceived difference grew roughly linearly with activation for most AUs; almost no AU was distinguishable from neutral at 0.2 activation except eyes closed and mouth open.
Geometric RMS predicted visibility better than the image metric SSIM; character race/sex had some effects, no other-race effect.
practical_applications: Subtle face moves (<20% intensity) are invisible to viewers - at our small on-screen sizes push face changes harder or move the body instead.
limitations: Realistic virtual humans viewed close-up; stylised 2D puppets not tested.

title: Principles of traditional animation applied to 3D computer animation
key_findings: Lists the Disney principles (squash & stretch, timing, anticipation, staging, follow-through/overlap, straight-ahead vs pose-to-pose, slow in/out, arcs, exaggeration, secondary action, appeal).
Staging in silhouette: early black-and-white characters showed that actions must read in silhouette; Andre's scratch was moved to the side for clarity.
Anticipation prepares the audience and can show weight (bend low before lifting a heavy object).
'All actions and movements of a character are the result of its thought processes'; a character does the same action differently in different emotional states.
Exaggeration must be balanced across design, action, sound; exaggerating only one element - or everything - looks wrong.
practical_applications: Silhouette test for every key pose of Mint & Tao; show the thought before the action.
limitations: Craft knowledge from a practitioner (Pixar), published at SIGGRAPH; not empirical evidence.

title: Acting for Animators (5th edition)
key_findings: Publisher description/TOC: applies acting theory (Aristotle to Stanislavsky) to animation; action -> obstacle -> objective; 'acting is a process of exposing, not of hiding'; acting is doing and reacting; status transactions and power centres; psychological gesture; character rhythm; a scene is a negotiation; Laban movement analysis.
Earlier edition TOC (retailer listing, 4th ed. 2017) includes 'Thinking tends to lead to conclusions' and 'Emotion tends to lead to action'.
practical_applications: Give every character an objective and an obstacle per scene; stage status changes through posture and space.
limitations: Only publisher/retailer pages read; book content not read; practitioner tier.
